cim: Nvidia turmoil adds to Wall Street's growing fears about the AI boom
kihagyva: P3: 47 pont, tendencia 17%, jóváhagyás után fordul
cim_eredeti: Nvidia turmoil adds to Wall Street's growing fears about the AI boom
szoveg_eredeti:
by AUSTIN DENEAN | The National News Desk

WASHINGTON (TNND) — Stocks tied to the artificial intelligence industry have continued on their rollercoaster over the last week as markets swing widely over fears of an industry letdown and turmoil at country’s most valuable company after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned and was subsequently reinstated by its board.

Markets ended last week in correction territory driven by a harsh slowdown in tech stocks, including a 50% drop-off for Nvidia that had accelerated in the days after Huang’s departure from the company.

Huang’s return to Nvidia sparked a rally on Monday, including a recovery of the company own share prices, that fizzled out again as worries about the AI industry overrode optimism about his return and its impact on the company’s future success.

The recent selloffs in AI stocks aren’t the first sign of trouble for the industry on Wall Street. In October, stock in Google parent company Alphabet lost $500 billion in a day after it reported it could take longer than expected to turn a profit on AI. Anthropic, the Claude developer that just had a historic initial public offering, has seen its share prices fall below their initial list price.

That turmoil has highlighted how much of Wall Street’s enthusiasm for AI is depending on sustained growth in spending, rising valuations that may be reaching a peak and whether the biggest companies can eventually turn profits on their massive investments. Even before the turmoil at the top of Nvidia, investors were becoming more concerned the industry was taking on too much debt and spending too much without a clear bath to generating sufficient returns.

Investors have grown skeptical of seemingly endless demands for capital to fund data center construction across the industry. Trillions of dollars have been pledged across the tech ecosystem, much of which increasingly dependent on borrowing and complicated financing arrangements.

More than half of fund managers in a Bank of America survey this month expect at least one major AI company to cut capital spending within the next six months, up from 30% in October. The survey also found a record share of fund managers believe companies are overinvesting, while investors sharply reduced their exposure to technology stocks.

Nvidia is at the center of those arrangements, as Huang frequently offered financial aid to cash-strapped customers by making deals to buy computing capacity or other services in return in what is known as circular financing. The International Monetary Fund estimates circular financing among AI companies has grown to over $1 trillion, about two-thirds of which is funded by debt.

Other Silicon Valley leaders that pushed for Huang’s return to Nvidia highlighted his willingness to make deals to help the industry and warned his absence could jeopardize agreements supporting the AI expansion.

“Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract,” Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk wrote on X. “Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost.”

Higher interest rates are making those debts more expensive to finance and harder for companies to get access to capital. The Federal Reserve is also widely expected to raise interest rates next month and is weighing further increases next year to tame inflation that is nearly double its target, which would add to those challenges.

Markets have also questioned whether stock prices for AI and related companies shot too high and whether robust demand for memory, processing and other inputs for data centers could eventually lead to a supply glut if the industry’s expansion outpaces demand for its products, leaving companies with an oversupply of equipment, underutilized data centers and debts that become harder to repay.

The consequences of a deeper downturn would extend well beyond the tech industry, as AI-related companies account for a significant share of stock market gains and are increasingly prominent in retirement account holdings that could be exposed to losses if stock prices keep falling.

More Fed officials have also increasingly warned about those risks as the AI buildout becomes more dependent on debt. Fed Governor Michael Barr said earlier this month a sharp reversal in investor confidence could trigger forced asset sales and fuel financial instability, and Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman warned disappointing returns could bring a significant stock market correction.

AI’s financial challenges are also being deepened by political opposition to data centers, threatening to slow projects worth billions of dollars. Voters overwhelmingly backed ballot measures restricting construction of data centers and elected lawmakers who supported reining them in through moratoriums or other limitations.

Trump’s deep involvement in Huang’s reinstatement at Nvidia is also likely to ramp up congressional scrutiny of the company, creating new risks for one of the most powerful players in the industry. Democrats, who will soon have majorities in both chambers, universally panned Trump’s intervention and indicated it would become subject to congressional scrutiny.

Democratic lawmakers set to take over committee gavels already had planned to investigate Huang’s relationships and whether the company had failed to abide by export controls on chip sales to China, an effort that will be intensified with the White House’s involvement.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said on Monday that Democrats “will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain.”
